context_blurb:
Everything you can touch, from beach sand to the air in your lungs, is made of atoms, particles far too small to see. Chemists write each substance as a formula: a row of symbols and small numbers telling which atoms it holds, and how many.

An element is a pure substance made of only one kind of atom. Atoms often bond into small groups called molecules. The oxygen in air comes as molecules of two oxygen atoms, O2. Ozone, O3, has three to a molecule; it is a pale blue gas that irritates the lungs, yet high in the sky a layer of it soaks up nearly all of the Sun's harmful ultraviolet light. Because ozone and ordinary oxygen hold nothing but oxygen atoms, they are two forms of one element, even though their atoms are bonded together.

A compound is two or more different elements bonded in a fixed ratio, and it seldom behaves like the elements that built it. Sodium is a metal soft enough to cut with a knife, and it reacts violently with water; chlorine is a choking yellow-green gas. Joined one to one, they make sodium chloride, the salt every human body needs. As a compound, salt has properties all its own: it is stable, unreactive and safe to eat in moderate amounts.

Halve a drop of water again and again, and even a droplet far too small to see still holds countless molecules. The halving ends at a single molecule of water, one oxygen atom bonded to two hydrogen atoms, the smallest particle that keeps water's makeup and chemical properties. There is no water atom: break the molecule, and only hydrogen and oxygen are left.

Each symbol is one or two letters, a capital first and any second letter small, so every capital starts a new symbol. Co, with a small o, is therefore one symbol for one element: cobalt, a hard, bluish-grey metal. CO, with two capitals, is carbon and oxygen, the poisonous gas carbon monoxide, and copper is Cu, from its Latin name, cuprum.

A small number after a symbol counts the atoms of that element alone, and a symbol with no number means one atom. Ammonia, the sharp-smelling gas of rotting matter, is NH3. Each of its molecules is one nitrogen atom joined to three hydrogen atoms, since the 3 belongs to the hydrogen alone. Glucose, the sugar that fuels the body's cells, is C6H12O6. Its formula holds only three symbols, so glucose is built from three elements, carbon, hydrogen and oxygen; the numbers count its atoms, six, twelve and six, twenty-four in all. In quartz, the main mineral of sand, silicon and oxygen atoms link into one network through the whole crystal. So its formula, SiO2, gives a ratio, not a count: two oxygen atoms for every silicon atom.

A battery shows what water holds. A current passed through water splits it into its two elements, which bubble off at two wires into two tubes, and the hydrogen tube always gathers twice as much gas. The reason is the molecule: each water molecule holds two hydrogen atoms for every oxygen atom, so splitting water frees twice as much hydrogen. Both gases come as two-atom molecules, and, as Amedeo Avogadro proposed in 1811, equal volumes of gases at the same temperature and pressure hold equal numbers of molecules, however light or heavy the gas.

Around 1800 the French chemist Joseph Proust prepared copper carbonate himself and compared it with the same compound dug up as a mineral. Both held about five parts copper to one of carbon and four of oxygen by mass. A compound, Proust concluded, always holds its elements in fixed proportions, though the parts need not be equal. Claude Berthollet, another French chemist, argued that the makeup depends on how a compound forms, but by the 1810s the evidence had settled the debate for Proust.

In 1808 the English chemist John Dalton built such findings into a theory of atoms. Each element has its own kind of atom, he said, and atoms are never created, destroyed or changed into another element's atoms, though alchemists had long believed one metal could be turned into another. In Dalton's view, a bar of pure gold holds gold atoms only, all alike and all of the same weight. Later chemists found that most elements' atoms come in a few slightly different weights, though gold's really are all alike.
